title: Robert Kiyosaki Says He Lost Everything—and It Was a Good Thing
summary: Robert Kiyosaki says losing everything was beneficial when mistakes became lessons instead of lasting bitterness. His account of repeated setbacks highlights how sudden riches can disappear through ego or misplaced trust. Why Kiyosaki Viewed Losing Everything as Beneficial Losing everything offered ...
content:
Robert Kiyosaki says losing everything was beneficial when mistakes became lessons instead of lasting bitterness. His account of repeated setbacks highlights how sudden riches can disappear through ego or misplaced trust.

Key Takeaways

  • Kiyosaki identifies ego and dishonest people as risks to sudden riches.
  • He describes experiencing all five of his initial money problems.
  • He calls losing everything a good thing if it becomes a life lesson.

Why Kiyosaki Viewed Losing Everything as Beneficial

Losing everything offered an opportunity to develop better financial judgment, Robert Kiyosaki, author of Rich Dad Poor Dad, explained in an Oct. 16 statement on X. He credited his rich dad with teaching him to turn setbacks into life lessons and become more financially intelligent instead of bitter.

Reflecting on his lessons from losing everything, Kiyosaki wrote:

“I’ve experience this too, several times. The good news is, losing everything was a good thing for me.”

He framed the benefit as conditional on recognizing an error and growing from it, making the response to failure central to his account.

His criticism of schools followed that distinction, accusing the education system of punishing mistakes instead of teaching people to examine them. He argued that fear of errors or failure to learn from past decisions can contribute to poverty. Kiyosaki added: “Humans were designed to make mistakes, learn, and grow smarter.”

Everyone Has Money Problems, Including the Wealthy

Everyone has money problems, Kiyosaki argued in his five-part list of financial challenges, also published Oct. 16. These were having none, earning too little, spending more than one earns, lacking funds for the future, and having too much. He said:

“I have had all five problems.”

The famous author maintained that solving the first four taught him lessons that left him facing a different problem: having too much money.

His follow-up introduced a sixth problem: going from sudden riches to having nothing, a transition he associated with inflated egos or dishonest people gaining access to assets. Professional athletes, movie stars, lottery winners, and inheritance recipients were among his examples. He named managers, accountants, attorneys, and relatives as potential sources of dishonesty.

Practicing decisions with play money was the purpose Kiyosaki gave for creating the Cashflow board game with Kim Kiyosaki. Players buy assets, evaluate investment opportunities, and track the effects of their choices. His closing advice was: “Make mistakes, learn, grow, and enjoy a richer life.”

From Financial Education to Protecting Wealth

Kiyosaki’s approach to rebuilding begins with improving financial judgment before putting money at risk. Discussing a hypothetical $10,000 rebuilding plan in July, he prioritized financial knowledge, mentorship, and income-producing skills before buying investments.

For older savers, a major loss can also leave less time to recover before retirement. In his retirement savings warning, posted Sept. 27 on X, he predicted that severe declines in stocks and bonds could leave some baby boomers without enough time to rebuild their savings.

Preparing for economic trouble is a precaution comparable to carrying car insurance, Kiyosaki argued in an Oct. 3 statement. He outlined his financial preparedness approach while reiterating his preference for gold, silver, and bitcoin over government-issued currency.

He favors those holdings as protection against currency depreciation and financial instability, citing excessive debt and loose monetary policy. In a March 16 statement, Kiyosaki predicted bitcoin would reach $750,000 one year after the global financial crash he anticipated.

Buying bitcoin to preserve savings still exposes investors to price declines, even when their concern is a weakening currency. Its limited supply supports the argument for bitcoin as an inflation hedge, but demand and market conditions also determine its value. Holders can lose purchasing power if its price falls while living costs rise.

title: Bitcoin rally could revive treasury buying, but easy-money days over
summary: “A return to last year’s indiscriminate capital raising looks unlikely,” said Bitfinex head of derivatives Jag Kooner.
content:
Corporate Bitcoin purchases could accelerate toward the end of 2026 and into 2027 if the cryptocurrency rallies, but investors are likely to be more selective about which treasury companies they finance, according to analysts. 

Speaking to Cointelegraph, Bitwise head of research Ryan Rasmussen said there was a broad slowdown in Bitcoin treasury buying in Q3. Strategy’s Bitcoin holdings increased by a net 1,666 BTC in Q3, down from 83,901 BTC in Q2, according to company filings. Other public companies added a net 5,617 BTC, compared with 45,725 BTC in the previous quarter, according to figures supplied by Rasmussen. 

Rasmussen said he expects a re-acceleration of corporate Bitcoin purchases to begin as early as this year. Bitfinex head of derivatives Jag Kooner said renewed buying could follow if treasury companies regain premiums to the value of their Bitcoin holdings, allowing them to issue shares and acquire more Bitcoin without diluting existing shareholders’ Bitcoin exposure per share. 

The model became popular during the 2025 treasury boom, when companies could raise capital by issuing shares at a premium to the value of their Bitcoin holdings. But as those premiums narrowed or disappeared, issuing new shares became less attractive, limiting companies’ ability to finance additional purchases. 

“Shareholders have seen premiums collapse and some companies sell into weakness. Investors are now pricing these businesses on funding costs, balance-sheet discipline and bitcoin per share,” said Kooner. 

“A rally could therefore restart buying, particularly among companies with credible financing structures but a return to last year’s indiscriminate capital raising looks unlikely.”

Established Bitcoin treasuries may get first access to capital 

Bitwise’s October market report also showed a decline in the number of Bitcoin treasuries in Q3, driven by smaller companies abandoning their Bitcoin treasury strategies. A dozen companies that entered during the 2025 treasury boom sold their entire holdings mostly to repay debt or return cash to shareholders after their stock premiums evaporated, said Rasmussen.

Kooner expects established players to attract capital first if buying resumes.

“Initially, capital would likely gravitate towards established players, which have the scale, the liquidity in their own securities and the track record investors now demand,” he said. 

Related: Bitcoin is rejected at $83K as US bond yields reverse higher with equities

Rasmussen said most of the largest corporate buyers outside Strategy were operating businesses adding Bitcoin from cash flow rather than issuing stock to fund purchases. That represents “a smaller source of demand but a healthier one,” he said.

Meanwhile, Kooner cautioned that a broader resurgence of new treasury-companies could emerge only after a rally is well underway.

“A broad wave of new listings would most likely arrive late in a rally, once premiums have widened and that timing is itself a warning sign.”

Bitcoin ETFs could support recovery without treasury boom 

Even without another corporate Bitcoin buying boom, Rasmussen said there will be other drivers for a Bitcoin recovery, pointing to $6.4 billion in spot Bitcoin net inflow in Q3. 

“Corporate purchases are one source of demand for bitcoin, but not the only source,” he said.

Kooner agreed ETF demand could sustain the recovery for a period, but cautioned that some activity reflects basis trades that can unwind quickly.

“Without corporate buying, the market loses a price-insensitive bid and becomes more dependent on allocators who rebalance with macro conditions,” he said.

Recent flows show that ETF demand can reverse. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded around $229 million in net outflows last week, their second consecutive week of net withdrawals, according to SoSoValue data.

title: Blackrock Files for Bitcoin ETF Designed to Limit Investor Losses
summary: Blackrock is seeking to launch a bitcoin ETF designed to cushion market losses while limiting potential gains. The proposed fund would use options and fixed-income investments instead of holding bitcoin directly. Blackrock Proposes Bitcoin ETF With Built-In Downside Protection Bitcoin investors coul...
content:
Blackrock is seeking to launch a bitcoin ETF designed to cushion market losses while limiting potential gains. The proposed fund would use options and fixed-income investments instead of holding bitcoin directly.

Key Takeaways

  • Blackrock files for the Ishares Bitcoin Managed Protection ETF (PBIT).
  • The strategy targets an initial 10% loss threshold per tranche, not a guaranteed limit for shareholders.
  • Investors would sacrifice some potential gains in exchange for downside protection.

Blackrock Proposes Bitcoin ETF With Built-In Downside Protection

Bitcoin investors could gain access to a new exchange-traded fund (ETF) designed to reduce exposure to sharp market declines under a proposal filed by Blackrock. The world’s largest asset manager submitted a registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Oct. 19 for the Ishares Bitcoin Managed Protection ETF, which would trade under the ticker PBIT.

The proposed fund would seek gains linked to the Ishares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) or similar bitcoin-linked assets while seeking to provide a level of downside protection. Unlike traditional spot bitcoin ETFs, PBIT would not directly hold bitcoin or bitcoin exchange-traded products. Instead, it would use options contracts and fixed-income securities.

Investors can gain bitcoin exposure through ETFs without directly owning the cryptocurrency. PBIT would introduce a different approach, limiting potential gains to help cushion losses. However, shareholders could still lose some or all of their investment.

How Blackrock’s Bitcoin ETF Would Limit Potential Losses

The proposed fund would generally use three overlapping sets of options contracts, known as tranches, starting in different months. Each tranche would combine purchased call options, which provide the right to buy an asset at a predetermined price, with sold calls that cap gains above a specified price, called the strike price.

Call options would generally be purchased with strike prices approximately 10% below the reference asset’s starting value. The reference asset, such as IBIT, is the investment the options are tied to. This structure would initially limit losses to approximately 10% of that asset’s starting value for each tranche, before expenses.

That protection would not guarantee a 10% maximum loss for shareholders. Thresholds could change, and losses measured from a higher market value could exceed the initial limit. The fund expects to use Flexible Exchange Options (FLEX Options), exchange-traded contracts with customizable terms, and may adjust its options positions as market conditions change.

The strategy would also include cash, money market funds, short-term government obligations, and investment-grade fixed-income securities. Interest income could help cover options costs and offset some losses.

Bitcoin ETF Would Cap Gains in Exchange for Protection

Selling call options would generate payments to help finance the protective strategy, while restricting returns during bitcoin rallies. PBIT could therefore underperform bitcoin in rising markets, with volatility and trading expenses potentially weakening its downside protection.

The existing Ishares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) seeks to reflect bitcoin’s price performance without employing the proposed managed protection strategy. The fund held approximately $65.34 billion in net assets as of Oct. 16, according to Blackrock’s published figures.

An earlier filing for a bitcoin income ETF, submitted Jan. 23, outlined a fund holding bitcoin and IBIT shares while selling call options for income.

A subsequent Form 8-A filing in June preceded the planned Nasdaq listing of its income-focused bitcoin product. The strategy uses covered calls to collect payments while limiting some potential gains.

The same income product launched June 16 as the Ishares Bitcoin Premium Income ETF (BITA). While BITA emphasizes income generation, PBIT would focus on downside protection.

Blackrock’s New Bitcoin ETF Faces Regulatory Process

A post-effective amendment to an existing Ishares Trust registration statement proposes that it become effective 75 days after Oct. 19. The preliminary prospectus prohibits sales until the registration becomes effective.

Responsibility for managing the ETF would fall to Blackrock Fund Advisors, and the filing flags risks involving options liquidity, interest rates, and counterparty exposure, the risk that another party fails to meet its financial obligations. Under its 80% investment policy, the fund would normally allocate at least 80% of net assets, plus investment borrowings, to bitcoin exposure or its protection strategy.

The management fee remains unspecified. Expenses would reduce returns, while changing options positions could produce different outcomes depending on when shareholders invest.

title: UK Men Get Prison Time for Violent Home Invasion Targeting Crypto Holder
summary: Bristol Crown Court sentenced three men to prison for a botched cryptocurrency robbery attempt that left the victim with severe injuries.   Failed Crypto Heist Turns Violent Bristol Crown Court on Oct. 15 sentenced three men to prison terms ranging from five to six years for an aggravated burglary a...
content:
Bristol Crown Court sentenced three men to prison for a botched cryptocurrency robbery attempt that left the victim with severe injuries.

Key Takeaways

  • Bristol Crown Court sentenced three men up to six years in prison for a May 15 crypto-related home invasion.
  • The case reflects a rise in U.K. robberies targeting investors who store millions in digital assets.
  • Law enforcement including PC Gemma Childs praised quick-thinking witnesses who prevented further harm.

Failed Crypto Heist Turns Violent

Bristol Crown Court on Oct. 15 sentenced three men to prison terms ranging from five to six years for an aggravated burglary after they forced their way into a home, assaulted a man, and demanded cryptocurrency.

According to a police report, two of the men, Terroll Paul, 31, and Pierre Madzou, 30, both of Barking, London, were sentenced to six years and five-and-a-half years in prison, respectively. The third, Mohamed Samagassi, 37, of no fixed address, received a five-year sentence. All three men pleaded guilty in August to charges of aggravated burglary.

The police said the trio broke into the victim’s Bristol home in the early hours of May 15 in a failed attempt to steal digital currency. During the attack, the victim was struck over the head, sustaining a substantial injury that required hospital treatment. The suspects were arrested at the scene after the victim’s teenage sister alerted police.

The sentencing comes amid a concerning surge in violent U.K. robberies targeting individuals believed to hold significant wealth in cryptocurrency. In one recent case, assailants targeted an unidentified businessman and his pregnant wife in their home. In September, another British court heard evidence detailed against a cybercriminal who orchestrated a series of violent home invasions across the country, attempting to extort millions of dollars in cryptocurrency from high-net-worth holders.

Impact on the Victim and Police Praise

Meanwhile, in a victim personal statement read during the sentencing hearing, the unnamed victim said the attack drastically changed his demeanor and left him constantly frightened.

“Before, I was bubbly, talkative, and outgoing, but now I would describe myself as tense and apprehensive,” the victim said.

PC Gemma Childs, the investigating officer, praised the resilience of both the victim and his younger sister.

“The victim’s younger sister has also shown extreme bravery, with her actions leading directly to the apprehension of the offenders and preventing her brother from further harm,” Childs said. “This is something that no one should have to go through in their lives, especially not a child, and her quick thinking in this situation is nothing short of remarkable.”

title: Zcash Proposes New Privacy Layer to Guard Swaps From Quantum Risks
summary: Zakura has proposed a new privacy safeguard for zcash swaps routed through Near Intents, designed to stop future quantum computers from linking one exposed refund address to a user’s wider transaction history. Zakura Proposes One-Key-Per-Swap Privacy for Zcash Quantum computers are not cracking Zcas...
content:
Zakura has proposed a new privacy safeguard for zcash swaps routed through Near Intents, designed to stop future quantum computers from linking one exposed refund address to a user’s wider transaction history.

Key Takeaways

  • Zakura proposed one-time viewing keys for every zcash swap routed through Near Intents.
  • The design limits future quantum exposure to one swap without changing users’ spending keys.
  • With $19M+ routed into ZEC, privacy hardening is becoming a practical infrastructure priority.

Zakura Proposes One-Key-Per-Swap Privacy for Zcash

Quantum computers are not cracking Zcash today. Yet, Zcash developer Zakura is already designing around the possibility that one eventually could.

The Zcash infrastructure team has proposed a one-time incoming viewing key for every ZEC swap through Near Intents, addressing a subtle privacy risk created when shielded Zcash addresses are posted permanently on Near’s public blockchain.

Today, multiple diversified Zcash addresses can share the same underlying incoming viewing key. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer using Shor’s algorithm could theoretically recover that key from a publicly exposed address and use it to link payments received across the account.

Zakura’s proposal limits the blast radius.

One Swap, One Viewing Key

Under the design, every cross-chain swap receives a separate incoming viewing key and refund address.

If quantum technology eventually breaks one publicly posted address, then an attacker would learn about payments associated with that swap alone, rather than gaining visibility into the account’s broader payment history.

Crucially, the user’s spending key does not change. Funds received through the one-time address remain spendable from the same account, avoiding the cumbersome alternative of creating separate Zcash accounts for every transaction.

That distinction is important for both software and hardware wallets, where splitting funds across numerous accounts could create serious usability problems.

Private Lookups Solve the Recovery Problem

Creating a new viewing key for every swap introduces another challenge: wallet recovery.

A restored wallet would otherwise have to scan Zcash history repeatedly using every swap key it had ever generated.

Zakura proposes solving this with private information retrieval (PIR). Public filters help determine whether a refund address received funds, while encrypted queries allow the wallet to locate the relevant transaction without the server learning which address is being checked.

Compatible software wallets using Zakura’s open-source libraries could integrate the feature within weeks, with hardware-wallet support expected later.

Near Intents Usage Makes the Risk Worth Solving

This is not merely theoretical infrastructure with no users.

In September, Aurora Intents processed more than $19 million across 1,718 swaps for a zcash-denominated zkSNARKs auction, demonstrating meaningful demand for cross-chain routes into ZEC.

That makes permanently published addresses a privacy issue worth addressing before quantum machines become capable of exploiting them.

Zcash developers are separately preparing the broader NU7 network upgrade, though the currently proposed NU7 changes are not themselves a comprehensive post-quantum migration.

The bigger signal is cultural: crypto security teams are increasingly treating quantum risk as something to engineer around now, not after the first practical attack appears.

title: Missouri Hits Polymarket and Kalshi With Cease-and-Desist Orders
summary: Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway stressed that prediction markets could not label sports bets as event contracts to skirt law compliance. The state sent letters to Polymarket, Kalshi, Crypto.com, Novig, Underdog, and Robinhood calling on them to stop offering these products to Missourians...
content:
1. News
  2. Regulation & Legal
  3. Missouri Hits Polymarket and Kalshi With Cease-and-Desist Orders

Published:Oct 19, 2026, 6:50 PM EDT

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway stressed that prediction markets could not label sports bets as event contracts to skirt law compliance. The state sent letters to Polymarket, Kalshi, Crypto.com, Novig, Underdog, and Robinhood calling on them to stop offering these products to Missourians or face enforcement actions.

WRITTEN BY

SHARE

Published: Oct 19, 2026, 6:50 PM EDT

Key Takeaways

  • Missouri ordered platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi to stop offering sports event markets in the state.
  • The state claims these contracts dodge sports gambling rules, license fees, and a 10% tax.
  • Operators face enforcement in 30 days, amplifying the legal fight between states and the CFTC.

Missouri Sends Cease-and-Desist Letters to Prediction Market Platforms

Missouri is targeting prediction market platforms that offer sports-linked event markets.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway announced that her office sent cease-and-desist letters to several companies operating platforms that let Missourians access these sports event contracts—elements that her office considers illegal under state law.

Polymarket, Kalshi, Crypto.com, Novig, Underdog, and Robinhood have been affected by these actions, as Hanaway labeled the provision of these services as operating an unlicensed sports wagering business.

In the letters sent to these event market operators, Hanaway claims that they have sought to avoid complying with similar sports gambling laws of other states by claiming that they offer “event contracts”—or so-called “swaps”—governed by the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) and subject to exclusive regulation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

Nonetheless, Missouri contests this assumption, supported by several federal court rulings that have decided that these bets do not qualify as “swaps” and escape CFTC oversight. The letters also stress that failing to comply with state laws has caused economic damages to Missouri, as the platforms have not paid license fees nor the 10% wagering tax that applies to adjusted gross revenue of all in-state sports wagering.

“Missourians voted for a safe, well‑regulated sports wagering market that supports public education and addresses problem gambling. Companies cannot repackage sports bets as ‘event contracts’ to avoid Missouri law. We will enforce the rules voters approved and protect consumers,” said Hanaway.

Prediction markets platforms will have 30 days to stop offering sports-based event contracts in the state, or risk facing enforcement actions.

Missouri’s action is the latest in a series of actions that have pitted states against prediction market platforms on whether sports event markets do constitute gambling products. On September 2, New Jersey directed a petition to the Supreme Court to determine whether federal law preempts states “from regulating sports bets that occur within their jurisdictions if those bets are offered on markets registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.”

While states have pushed back against the CFTC on the matter, the commission has reiterated that it retains exclusive oversight over these contracts. “To any state that seeks to nullify federal law and seize authority over these markets, I say again: We will see you in court,” said Chairman Michael S. Selig in April.

title: AnchorWatch Launches Nevada Trust Company, Caps Bitcoin Custody Fees at $10,000 a Month
summary:
Bitcoin Magazine

AnchorWatch Launches Nevada Trust Company, Caps Bitcoin Custody Fees at $10,000 a Month
AnchorWatch’s AnchorWatch Trust Company has now opened its custody service. 
This post AnchorWatch Launches Nevada Trust Company, Caps Bitcoin Custody Fees at $10,000 a Month first appeared on B...
content:
Bitcoin custody and insurance firm AnchorWatch has said that its Nevada state-chartered trust company opened for business, offering qualified custody for fiduciaries, public companies, trusts and high-net-worth individuals.

AnchorWatch Trust Company, authorized by the Nevada Financial Institutions Division to act as a custodian, opened on Monday, according to AnchorWatch. 

The service is aimed at public companies holding BTC, a category that has expanded sharply as more corporations have added the asset to their balance sheets.

The company’s flagship differentiator is pricing: fixed-dollar annual fees tiered by vault size, capped at $10,000 per month, rather than the percentage-of-assets charges typical among qualified custodians. Once a client hits the cap, additional bitcoin purchases or price appreciation do not increase the annual fee.

“For large enterprises, the pricing cap will translate to potential six- or seven-figure annual savings for qualified custody,” the company said in its announcement.

ATC offers clients two qualified-custody models. Flagship Custody, where ATC holds the keys required for qualified custody while the client’s trustees or executives hold additional keys, and multi-institution custody, where key control is distributed across three institutions — AnchorWatch Trust Company, BitGo in the United States, and CoinCorner in the Isle of Man.

The multi-institution model addresses a growing concern among institutional bitcoin holders: concentration risk at a single custodian, an anxiety sharpened by past industry failures.

Clients may also apply for insurance issued in the covered client’s or entity’s name — a structure AnchorWatch contrasts with policies held in the custodian’s name, where coverage terms may leave ambiguity about the client’s position in a claim. The insurance is provided by AnchorWatch and backed by A+ rated Lloyd’s of London syndicates.

As a Lloyd’s of London Coverholder, AnchorWatch says it has authority to write up to $370 million in limits per ATC client, covering loss of Bitcoin from perils including violent coercion and kidnapping, as well as losses arising from fraudulent acts by AnchorWatch itself. Coverage is subject to underwriting approval and policy terms.

Insurance is available to U.S.-domiciled companies and subsidiaries and U.S.-resident individuals. Custody without insurance may be available across a broader range of jurisdictions, subject to KYC and AML requirements.

AnchorWatch’s underlying custody platform, Trident Vault, has secured customer Bitcoin for 20 months, according to the company. It has been audited or reviewed by security firms Halborn and Doyensec, and by the technical underwriters at the Lloyd’s syndicates backing the policies. 

AnchorWatch describes itself as a Bitcoin-native insurance and custody company; ATC is its Nevada state-chartered trust company arm.

Mathew Di Salvo

Mathew is a reporter who's covered the space since 2019, reporting on everything from Salvadoran president Nayib Bukele's Bitcoin bet to crypto exchange FTX's bankruptcy.

title: Smashed Quantum Computing Record Raises Stakes for Bitcoin Security
summary: Quantum computing firm Quantinuum has announced a major breakthrough in error correction, achieving a record 99.9995% logical fidelity that it says strengthens its path toward a commercially viable, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029. The advance comes amid mounting concerns that increasingly p...
content:
Quantum computing firm Quantinuum has announced a major breakthrough in error correction, achieving a record 99.9995% logical fidelity that it says strengthens its path toward a commercially viable, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029. The advance comes amid mounting concerns that increasingly powerful quantum machines could eventually undermine the cryptography protecting bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.

Key Takeaways

  • Quantinuum achieved a record 99.9995% logical fidelity, reducing quantum error rates tenfold from September.
  • The breakthrough advances Quantinuum’s goal of delivering a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029.
  • Progress raises concerns for Bitcoin security, as powerful quantum computers could eventually break cryptographic protections, accelerating calls for quantum-resistant upgrades.

Quantum Accuracy Is Rapidly Improving

Quantinuum said Monday that its Helios quantum computer achieved a logical error rate of just five errors per million operations, a tenfold improvement over its previous record set in September. The company claims the result is also 100 times better than the best published result using competing quantum hardware architectures, previously reported by Google Quantum AI.

The breakthrough addresses one of quantum computing’s biggest challenges: keeping calculations accurate despite the extreme sensitivity of quantum bits, or qubits, to errors. Unlike conventional computers, quantum systems require sophisticated error-correction techniques to reliably perform complex calculations.

Quantinuum achieved the result using a technique known as a “color code,” which combines multiple physical qubits into more reliable logical qubits. The company’s researchers also demonstrated that errors declined exponentially as they increased the level of protection, with each tested increase reducing the remaining logical errors by a factor of 12.

The results build on Quantinuum’s September breakthrough, which used a different error-correction method on the same Helios hardware.

“We’ve crossed the threshold necessary for exponential improvements in accuracy, reinforcing our path to Apollo and how we can help users unlock commercial value from quantum at scale,” said Quantinuum CEO Rajeeb Hazra, in a statement.

The company said its latest achievement brings error-correction performance into the target range for Apollo, its planned universal fault-tolerant quantum computer expected by 2029.

Robin Blume-Kohout, co-director of Sandia National Laboratories’ Quantum Performance Lab, who was not involved in the research, called the achievement a significant milestone. He said the findings suggest a scaled-up system could achieve useful fault-tolerant computing with fewer than one million physical qubits.

The results nevertheless concern a specific error-correction benchmark rather than a demonstration of a large-scale, general-purpose quantum computer. Significant engineering challenges remain before such systems can execute complex algorithms reliably.

Bitcoin’s Quantum Threat Comes Into Focus

The announcement follows a separate breakthrough announced by Google Quantum AI last week, as researchers demonstrated a technique called “magic state cultivation” that reduced errors by a factor of 40. The research achieved 99.99% logical fidelity in producing specialized quantum states needed for certain advanced computations.

As Bitcoin.com News reported, Google’s progress has renewed concerns about “Q-Day,” the hypothetical point at which quantum computers become powerful enough to break widely used cryptographic systems.

Earlier this year, Google researchers estimated that breaking the elliptic-curve cryptography used in Bitcoin’s digital signatures could require fewer than 500,000 physical qubits, roughly 20 times fewer than some previous estimates.

The research also outlined a theoretical scenario in which an advanced quantum computer could derive a bitcoin private key from an exposed public key in approximately nine minutes.

Researchers estimated that about 6.9 million BTC—nearly one-third of the total possible supply of bitcoin—could be potentially vulnerable because their public keys have already been exposed, including funds held in older wallet formats and reused addresses.

Although Quantinuum’s latest breakthrough does not demonstrate any capability to crack Bitcoin’s cryptography, it represents progress toward the reliable quantum computation that could eventually make such attacks feasible.

The developments have intensified discussions about preparing cryptocurrency networks for a post-quantum world. Fidelity Digital Assets has warned that exposed Bitcoin public keys could become vulnerable, while Coinbase has highlighted the technical challenges of transitioning the Bitcoin network to quantum-resistant cryptography.

Potential defenses include new digital signature schemes, but implementing them could require substantial changes to Bitcoin’s infrastructure, including larger signatures, wallet upgrades, and coordination across the decentralized network.

A particularly difficult issue involves dormant bitcoin holdings whose owners may be unable to migrate their funds to quantum-resistant addresses.

For now, no existing quantum computer is capable of breaking Bitcoin’s cryptographic protections. But with Quantinuum targeting 2029 for its fault-tolerant Apollo system and Google making rapid progress on related technologies, the race to develop quantum-resistant cryptocurrency infrastructure is taking on greater urgency.

title: After Analysing Markets, Trading Platforms Turn to Analysing Traders
summary:
Trading platforms have spent years adding market data, charts and AI research tools. Two recent product rollouts turn the analysis in the opposite direction, using clients’ trading histories to examine the behaviour behind their results. 
CFI is connecting its TradeWise scoring tool with the Kaiana ...
content:
2026-10-19T23:10:00.000+02:00

Monday, 19/10/2026 | 21:10 GMT by Tanya Chepkova

  • CFI's TradeWise analyses clients’ trading histories to produce a behavioural score and explain the patterns through a conversational interface.
  • DXtrade's Notofin integration give brokers access to a third-party tool that combines account data with subjective information entered by the trader.

Trading platforms have spent years adding market data, charts and AI research tools. Two recent product rollouts turn the analysis in the opposite direction, using clients’ trading histories to examine the behaviour behind their results.

CFI is connecting its TradeWise scoring tool with the Kaiana AI assistant, while DXtrade has integrated Notofin as an optional behavioural-analysis module for brokers.

The products follow different models but share the same premise: profit and loss records say what happened, while behavioural data may help explain why.

CFI Turns a Score into a Conversation

CFI's TradeWise analyses recurring patterns in a client’s past activity and brings them together in a Trading Behaviour Score. Kaiana provides the conversational interface, allowing clients to ask what affected the score or how their behaviour changed over time.

For example, a client who notices a change after several trades could ask Kaiana what the analysis identified in their recent activity. The feature is designed to make previous decisions easier to examine.

“TradeWise brings greater visibility to trading habits and patterns, while Kaiana helps clients explore and understand those insights,” said Ziad Melhem, CEO of CFI Financial Group.

He mentioned that the broker had already introduced the tool as part of its AI ecosystem in an August interview with Finance Middle East .

The latest announcement provides more detail about its connection with Kaiana and confirms its rollout through the current version of CFI’s iOS and Android app, subject to availability in individual markets.

DXtrade Adds Journaling and Emotional Context

DXtrade has taken a different route by integrating Notofin, an external performance intelligence platform. Brokers licensing DXtrade can decide whether to add the service to their client offering.

Notofin automatically imports trading activity and combines it with information supplied by the trader, including journal entries, screenshots, execution context and emotions associated with individual decisions.

Its analytics are intended to identify recurring strengths, mistakes and departures from a trading plan. Traders can also review their consistency across areas such as risk discipline, timing and adherence to a strategy.

"The market has been analyzed from every angle; the trader has not. Our work with Devexperts brings that missing behavioral layer to the DXtrade ecosystem, helping traders understand not only what happened in their accounts, but how their decisions, execution, and emotions shaped the outcome," said Kaloyan Ivanov, Co-CEO of Notofin.

Can Behavioural Feedback Improve Results?

Neither announcement provides evidence that behavioural feedback improves trading outcomes. CFI has not published the methodology used to calculate its Trading Behaviour Score, preventing clients from independently reproducing or assessing it.

Notofin explains which types of information it analyses, but some of its conclusions depend on traders consistently and accurately recording their emotions and decision-making context. Its AI-assisted observations are therefore not equivalent to an objective assessment of trading ability.

AI can determine whether someone is a good trader, but it can help turn account history from a record of past trades into an ongoing source of client feedback.

CFI is connecting its TradeWise scoring tool with the Kaiana AI assistant, while DXtrade has integrated Notofin as an optional behavioural-analysis module for brokers.

The products follow different models but share the same premise: profit and loss records say what happened, while behavioural data may help explain why.

CFI Turns a Score into a Conversation

CFI's TradeWise analyses recurring patterns in a client’s past activity and brings them together in a Trading Behaviour Score. Kaiana provides the conversational interface, allowing clients to ask what affected the score or how their behaviour changed over time.

For example, a client who notices a change after several trades could ask Kaiana what the analysis identified in their recent activity. The feature is designed to make previous decisions easier to examine.

“TradeWise brings greater visibility to trading habits and patterns, while Kaiana helps clients explore and understand those insights,” said Ziad Melhem, CEO of CFI Financial Group.

He mentioned that the broker had already introduced the tool as part of its AI ecosystem in an August interview with Finance Middle East .

The latest announcement provides more detail about its connection with Kaiana and confirms its rollout through the current version of CFI’s iOS and Android app, subject to availability in individual markets.

DXtrade Adds Journaling and Emotional Context

DXtrade has taken a different route by integrating Notofin, an external performance intelligence platform. Brokers licensing DXtrade can decide whether to add the service to their client offering.

Notofin automatically imports trading activity and combines it with information supplied by the trader, including journal entries, screenshots, execution context and emotions associated with individual decisions.

Its analytics are intended to identify recurring strengths, mistakes and departures from a trading plan. Traders can also review their consistency across areas such as risk discipline, timing and adherence to a strategy.

"The market has been analyzed from every angle; the trader has not. Our work with Devexperts brings that missing behavioral layer to the DXtrade ecosystem, helping traders understand not only what happened in their accounts, but how their decisions, execution, and emotions shaped the outcome," said Kaloyan Ivanov, Co-CEO of Notofin.

Can Behavioural Feedback Improve Results?

Neither announcement provides evidence that behavioural feedback improves trading outcomes. CFI has not published the methodology used to calculate its Trading Behaviour Score, preventing clients from independently reproducing or assessing it.

Notofin explains which types of information it analyses, but some of its conclusions depend on traders consistently and accurately recording their emotions and decision-making context. Its AI-assisted observations are therefore not equivalent to an objective assessment of trading ability.

AI can determine whether someone is a good trader, but it can help turn account history from a record of past trades into an ongoing source of client feedback.

title: JPMorgan Brings JPM Coin to Ethereum as Wall Street Embrace Expands
summary: JPMorgan Chase is expanding its JPM Coin deposit token to Ethereum, bringing blockchain-based dollar payments to the world’s second-largest cryptocurrency network as traditional financial institutions increasingly embrace public blockchain infrastructure. JPMorgan Expands to Ethereum Mainnet The lar...
content:
JPMorgan Chase is expanding its JPM Coin deposit token to Ethereum, bringing blockchain-based dollar payments to the world’s second-largest cryptocurrency network as traditional financial institutions increasingly embrace public blockchain infrastructure.

Key Takeaways

  • JPMorgan is expanding JPM Coin to Ethereum, enabling institutional clients to make 24/7 dollar payments with near-instant settlement.
  • The move reflects growing Wall Street crypto adoption, with banks increasingly using public blockchains for payments and tokenized asset settlements.
  • JPMorgan said its blockchain network already processes over $7 billion daily.

JPMorgan Expands to Ethereum Mainnet

The largest U.S. bank announced Monday that JPM Coin, which represents U.S. dollar deposits held at JPMorgan, will become available to institutional clients on Ethereum. The move follows the token’s launch on Coinbase’s Base—an Ethereum Layer 2 scaling network—in November 2025 and marks another step in the bank’s efforts to modernize payments and settlement using blockchain technology.

JPM Coin enables participating clients to transfer funds around the clock, with transactions settling in seconds rather than taking days through conventional banking infrastructure.

According to Bloomberg, JPMorgan expects demand from large cryptocurrency companies seeking blockchain-based payment solutions, along with financial institutions requiring digital cash to settle transactions involving tokenized assets or provide collateral.

Emma Landriault, global head of Kinexys Labs at JPMorgan’s blockchain division, told Bloomberg that the expansion reflects growing convergence between traditional financial institutions and cryptocurrency companies.

“We’ve clearly been in a year of further convergence between Wall Street and crypto,” Landriault said, describing increasing collaboration between established banks and institutional blockchain businesses.

The bank selected Ethereum because of its substantial liquidity and existing adoption among institutional clients, Landriault said. Ethereum remains the largest decentralized finance blockchain by total value locked, with nearly $50 billion deposited in applications operating on the network, according to DefiLlama.

Although JPM Coin will operate on public blockchain infrastructure, access to the deposit token will remain restricted to eligible institutional participants. Unlike conventional stablecoins, which are typically backed by reserves of cash and other liquid assets, deposit tokens represent claims on deposits held at the issuing bank.

Wall Street’s Blockchain Embrace Continues

The expansion comes as major financial companies accelerate efforts to tokenize traditional assets, including stocks, bonds, and investment funds. Blockchain-based settlement could allow financial institutions to move money and securities more efficiently while reducing reliance on traditional payment systems and their operating hours.

JPMorgan has emerged as one of the banking industry’s most active blockchain developers. Its Kinexys Blockchain Deposit Account network already facilitates transfers involving dollars, euros, pounds, and other currencies through the bank’s private blockchain infrastructure.

That network currently processes more than $7 billion in transactions daily, according to JPMorgan. However, that figure remains relatively small compared with the approximately $12 trillion in daily payment volume handled by the bank’s broader payments business.

By extending JPM Coin to Ethereum after its earlier Base deployment, JPMorgan is positioning its deposit token to serve financial institutions operating across both traditional banking systems and public blockchain networks.

title: Solana treasury firm SkyAI sells all SOL holdings, launches $201M buyback
summary: The former medical device maker has liquidated its Solana treasury and is offering to repurchase shares and warrants using its $223.8 million cash holdings.
content:
SkyAI, formerly Sharps Technology, has sold its entire Solana (SOL) treasury and launched a tender offer to repurchase up to $201.3 million in shares and warrants, reversing its cryptocurrency accumulation strategy.

The company held approximately $223.8 million in cash as of Oct. 16 after liquidating its SOL holdings, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.

The tender offer allows shareholders and warrant holders to sell their securities directly back to SkyAI at a fixed price. It covers up to 95% of each class of the company’s outstanding shares and warrants, funded entirely by cash on hand.

The company said the tender offer is no longer tied to SOL’s price, a condition it had initially planned to include when announcing the buyback on Oct. 11. SkyAI intends to continue developing a financial platform combining stablecoin infrastructure on Solana with artificial intelligence.

SkyAI shares closed Monday at $2.79, up 5.3% on the day, according to Yahoo Finance data. The stock has gained approximately 65% over the past month but remains down about 41% over the past year.

Related: Solana shows resilience, but some areas need continued observation, Fidelity says

SkyAI reverses Solana treasury strategy after one year

SkyAI launched its Solana treasury strategy in August 2025 after raising more than $400 million through a private placement. The company acquired more than 2 million SOL the following month, establishing a position valued at more than $400 million at the time.

By the end of 2025, the company held approximately 2.08 million SOL with a cost basis of $403.1 million, or roughly $194 per token. Its holdings were valued at $250.1 million, representing approximately $153 million in unrealized losses, according to its annual financial disclosures.

The losses reflected broader pressure on companies that accumulated SOL as a treasury asset. By February 2026, publicly traded Solana treasury companies faced more than $1.5 billion in combined unrealized losses as falling token prices weighed on their holdings and share valuations.

SOL fell to around $62 in June but has since recovered, trading near $104 as of Monday, according to CoinGecko data.

South Korea is approaching another decision point on its long-delayed cryptocurrency gains tax, with exchanges and policymakers preparing to discuss whether the January 2027 start date is realistic.

TL;DR: The country’s planned crypto tax has already been deferred three times. A new proposal would push implementation toward 2029, but no additional delay has been enacted.

Finance officials are expected to meet representatives of major domestic exchanges on October 20. The industry is arguing that the systems needed to handle different transaction types and calculate cost bases are still incomplete. A rushed launch, exchanges say, risks creating inconsistent tax treatment or driving activity to offshore platforms.

South Korea’s planned rate is commonly described as 22% after local tax is included, rather than a simple 20% all-in charge. The question now is less about whether crypto gains should ever be taxable than whether the supporting reporting infrastructure is ready for millions of transactions across different venues.

A lawmaker’s proposal would link the effective date to cross-border data sharing through the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, potentially moving the start to 2029. That measure requires legislative action; a meeting with exchanges cannot, by itself, change the law.

For investors, the current scheduled date remains January 2027 unless lawmakers decide otherwise. For exchanges, a later timetable could buy time to build reporting systems, but another postponement would also prolong policy uncertainty. South Korea has reached this crossroads before, which is why a proposed delay should not be reported as a settled outcome.

title: Crypto PAC pours $362K into California race voters essentially decided in August
summary: A Fairshake affiliate is supporting incumbent Aisha Wahab through ads in November, but the congresswoman already won a special election in the district.
content:
Protect Progress, an affiliate of the cryptocurrency-aligned Fairshake super political action committee (PAC), reported spending $362,000 on ads to support a Democrat in California’s 14th congressional district, just weeks after she won a special election against the same opponent. 

According to a Sunday filing with the US Federal Election Commission (FEC), Protect Progress reported spending $362,000 on media supporting incumbent Democrat Aisha Wahab in the Bay Area district against her fellow party member, Melissa Hernandez.

Wahab defeated Hernandez in an Aug. 18 special election with more than 53% of the vote, raising questions about why the cryptocurrency industry-aligned PAC is supporting her in the 2026 midterms. 

Notably, both Wahab and Hernandez were ranked as “strongly supports crypto” after they went on the record with the digital asset organization Stand With Crypto to complete questionnaires ahead of the August special election. That election was used to determine who would replace Democrat Eric Swalwell for the remainder of his term, ending January 2027. Swalwell resigned in April amid sexual assault allegations. 

Fairshake launched in 2023, backed largely by contributions from Coinbase, Ripple Labs and Andreessen Horowitz. Since the 2024 US elections, the Super PAC has spent tens of millions of dollars on candidates the group considers “pro-crypto” in efforts to fill Congress with lawmakers more likely to support policies favorable to the digital asset industry.  

Related: Ex-Trump crypto adviser profited after helping pass stablecoin bill: WSJ

In an Oct. 7 debate, Wahab signaled that she opposed Hernandez for not denouncing expenditures from corporate PACs aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), adding that the spending “really deteriorated our democracy.” Cointelegraph reached out to both the Hernandez and Wahab campaigns, and Fairshake for comment on the spending but did not receive immediate responses.

One notable change between the August special election and the November midterms will be the boundaries of California’s 14th district. The current boundaries, which include parts of San Francisco’s East Bay, will be expanded in accordance with the 2025 passage of the state’s Proposition 50, requiring new maps for the midterm elections.

Fairstake steps up spending in Ohio and Nebraska

The crypto PAC reported in January that it had $193 million in cash on hand ahead of the elections, and it had already used tens of millions of dollars to support Democratic and Republican candidates in primaries and special elections. 

With just over two weeks until the 2026 election, Fairshake reported additional spending on media for Senate races in Ohio and Nebraska. 

Defend American Jobs, a Fairshake affiliate largely supporting Republican candidates, reported spending more than $6.7 million to oppose Independent candidate Dan Osborn in Nebraska’s Senate race. The PAC also reported $8 million on media in Ohio, supporting incumbent Republican Jon Husted against Democrat Sherrod Brown in a race where it has spent more than $46 million so far. 

Brown’s race could be another bellwether for how the crypto industry potentially impacts the 2026 midterms. The Democrat lost his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 after Fairshake and other interest groups spent a combined hundreds of millions of dollars on ads opposing Brown.

title: Visa and Mesh Seek to End the Separate Crypto Card Requirement
summary: Mesh and Visa are joining forces to let consumers spend cryptocurrency and stablecoins at more than 175 million merchant locations without obtaining a separate crypto card or manually converting their holdings into cash. Announced Monday, the partnership connects digital wallets to Visa’s global pay...
content:
Mesh and Visa are joining forces to let consumers spend cryptocurrency and stablecoins at more than 175 million merchant locations without obtaining a separate crypto card or manually converting their holdings into cash. Announced Monday, the partnership connects digital wallets to Visa’s global payments network, although the companies have yet to disclose participating platforms or a launch date.

Key Takeaways

  • Mesh and Visa announced plans to enable crypto spending across more than 175 million merchant locations.
  • Mesh will handle payment conversion, eliminating the need for customers to manually cash out.
  • Visa and Mesh have not announced a launch date, participating platforms or supported devices.

Mesh and Visa Want to Turn Crypto Wallets Into Everyday Payment Tools

A cryptocurrency wallet holding bitcoin or stablecoins might soon work at the same checkout terminal that accepts an ordinary Visa card. On Monday, Mesh announced a partnership with Visa designed to unlock digital asset spending across more than 175 million merchant locations in over 200 countries and territories.

The arrangement promises something cryptocurrency payments have struggled to deliver for years: spending directly from existing wallet balances without opening another account, ordering a dedicated card or manually cashing out beforehand.

No Crypto Card, No New Checkout Equipment

Under the proposed arrangement, Mesh will connect participating cryptocurrency wallets and platforms to payment giant Visa’s infrastructure, allowing customers to tap at contactless terminals or complete online purchases using existing balances. Behind the scenes, a Visa payment credential handles the transaction while Mesh coordinates funding and conversion across supported cryptocurrencies, fiat-pegged stablecoins, and fiat currencies.

Merchants receive conventional payments without installing additional equipment or changing their checkout procedures. “Crypto never had a spending problem—it has a last-mile problem, and until now, closing it meant getting a separate card,” said Mesh CEO and co-founder Bam Azizi.

A $14.2 Trillion Network Meets Digital Wallets

Visa processed $14.2 trillion in payments during fiscal 2025, while cryptocurrency ownership reached an estimated 774 million people worldwide by June 2026, according to research cited in Mesh’s announcement. Yet cryptocurrency card spending reportedly amounted to approximately $1.5 billion monthly in late 2025, a comparatively modest figure compared to conventional payment volumes.

Mesh says more than 200 enterprises already use its network, which connects wallets, exchanges, and financial platforms.

The Missing Piece Is a Launch Date

Visa Global Head of Growth Rubail Birwadker remarked that the collaboration would expand how digital asset balances connect with established payment services. Mesh will manage onboarding and know-your-customer (KYC) procedures, allowing participating platforms to offer payments functionality without operating their own card programs.

However, neither company disclosed initial availability, supported devices, or participating platforms. Those details will arrive as rollout plans are finalized. For now, the partnership promises access to 175 million merchant locations, but consumers still don’t know when their wallets will actually work at checkout.

title: Here’s what happened in crypto today
summary: Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
content:
Today in crypto, Metaplanet secured shareholder approval to take a 93.7% stake in Nasdaq-listed Super League as part of its US expansion, World Liberty Financial’s USD1 stablecoin lost more than $400 million in market capitalization over two weeks and layer-1 blockchain Qubic halted its network after an attacker stole roughly $1.4 million from more than 1,400 wallets.

Metaplanet gains shareholder approval for US Bitcoin treasury expansion

Shareholders of Nasdaq-listed Super League have approved a transaction that would give Japanese Bitcoin treasury company Metaplanet a 93.7% ownership stake in exchange for 2,100 BTC and $2.5 million in cash.

Under the agreement, Metaplanet will receive nearly 45 million common shares, preferred stock carrying governance rights and warrants to purchase additional shares. The deal would give Metaplanet control of Super League’s board and major corporate decisions.

Super League plans to rebrand as Superplanet and trade under the ticker SUPA, shifting its business toward accumulating Bitcoin. The company intends to fund future purchases primarily through preferred stock offerings rather than conventional debt.

The transaction would also give Metaplanet access to US dollar-denominated capital markets, supplementing its existing fundraising activities in Japan. Metaplanet could invest an additional $210 million through junior preferred shares.

Metaplanet currently holds 44,000 BTC, making it the second-largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin holder behind Strategy. The company has also proposed allocating up to 15% of its assets to strategic investments aimed at supporting Bitcoin purchases and dividend payments.

World Liberty’s USD1 stablecoin sheds $400M in market cap

World Liberty Financial’s USD1 stablecoin has shed over $400 million in market capitalization over the past two weeks, driven by large redemptions on Ethereum and BNB Chain. 

On Monday, CoinGecko data showed USD1’s market capitalization at about $4.02 billion, down from $4.43 billion on Oct. 6. That’s a decline of approximately $401 million, or 9.1%. World Liberty Financial’s proof-of-reserves dashboard separately showed approximately $4.01 billion in reserves.

The decline extends a period of concentrated redemptions on Ethereum and BNB Chain, according to blockchain research firm Onchain Benchmark. The research platform found that nearly $200 million in BNB Chain redemptions originated from a single unidentified address, although it could not establish who controlled the funds or why they were redeemed.

Despite the redemptions, USD1 maintained its dollar peg throughout the period examined by Onchain Benchmark, trading between $0.998 and $1.000.

The researchers found no evidence of a sustained depegging event, indicating that the decline in circulating supply was not accompanied by a significant loss of the token’s dollar value.

Qubic freezes chain after attacker drains 1.4K wallets with weak seeds

Layer-1 blockchain network Qubic halted operations Sunday after an attacker reportedly exploited weakly generated wallet seeds to drain approximately $1.4 million from more than 1,400 accounts, according to the project. 

In a statement on X, Qubic said the network was halted at tick 85,371,949, where it remains paused at the time of writing. Qubic said the vulnerability affected wallet seeds generated using any browser on an iPhone or iPad, Safari on a Mac until Oct. 18, 2026, or the Qubic iOS app before July 2025, leading to 2.94 trillion Qubit (QU) stolen. 

“87.1% of the drained funds never left the Qubic network and remain frozen in place,” said Qubic. “The remaining 12.9% was sent to MEXC, whose team froze the receiving account within about an hour.” 

The Qubic theft is the latest in a series of attacks tied to weak wallet seeds. In July, Coldcard disclosed that attackers had stolen funds from wallets whose seeds were weakened by a firmware bug. Similar flaws affected Trust Wallet’s browser extension and the Libbitcoin Explorer tool in 2023.

Payward, the company behind crypto exchange Kraken, has agreed to acquire Lithuania-based Saldo Bank, taking a route into European banking that goes beyond obtaining another exchange registration.

TL;DR: The proposed acquisition would give Payward an existing licensed banking operation in Europe. The deal remains subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in 2027.

Saldo provides banking products including loans and deposits. Bringing it into Payward would potentially put cash accounts, crypto assets and lending under a more connected product offering, rather than forcing customers to move between a separate crypto venue and their bank every time they need to borrow, spend or settle funds.

This is an important difference from a cryptocurrency firm simply partnering with an external payments provider. Ownership of a bank brings a regulated operating business, supervisory obligations and a different level of responsibility for customer money. Payward will not acquire unrestricted banking powers across Europe merely by signing the purchase agreement; the necessary approval and post-acquisition controls are still ahead.

The European push also fits a wider industry pattern. Crypto companies are pursuing banking relationships and charters as tokenized securities, stablecoins and conventional financial accounts become more closely linked. Existing lenders, meanwhile, are building crypto products of their own.

For Kraken users, the immediate message is about direction rather than a product they can use today. A completed acquisition could eventually make financing and fiat services feel less fragmented. Until regulators approve the transaction and the integration is completed, the promised benefits remain plans rather than available services.

title: Market participants weigh in on SEC’s proposed crypto regulations
summary: The financial agency is scheduled to close public comments on its ‘Regulation Crypto Assets’ proposed in August.
content:
The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is set to move forward with digital asset policies after Congress failed to pass legislation that would have established a framework for regulating cryptocurrency at the agency and across other parts of government.

On Tuesday, the SEC will close to public comments on its ‘Regulation Crypto Assets,’ a set of rules proposed in August intended to create what the agency called a “clear and fit-for-purpose framework for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets.” Over the 60-day period, the agency gathered about 140 comments from interest groups and individuals on rules and regulations related to a proposed safe harbor that would prevent token issuers from being considered “investment contracts,” as well as exemptions for companies permitting offerings up to a certain amount.

The Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) Crypto Alliance, a group established to help organizations looking to implement the EU framework on digital assets, largely supported the SEC’s proposed changes to disclosure requirements. The alliance recommended specific amendments to have the SEC better define “concepts and data structures specific to crypto assets and the disclosure requirements.”

Others, including SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci, said they would support the SEC’s proposed crypto rules. Scaramucci said the digital asset regulations responded to “organic adoption” and “represent a return to the Commission’s proper role” without citing inaction from Congress on the Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act. Six people submitted comments anonymously.

While many public comments praised the SEC’s efforts to advance crypto regulation or said they would be open to further discussion, some legal experts suggest the rules could be more easily overturned than an act of Congress. Both financial agencies overseeing aspects of the crypto industry, the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, are also still understaffed at the leadership level.

Related: House Finance panel chair says regulator actions on crypto ‘fall short’ of CLARITY bill

title: The Architecture of Money: Mapping Financial Power in the Age of Bitcoin
summary:
Bitcoin Magazine

The Architecture of Money: Mapping Financial Power in the Age of Bitcoin
Carlijn Kingma, Thomas Bollen, and Martijn Jeroen van der Linden on The Waterworks of Money, the hidden structures of finance, and bitcoin's place in Europe's monetary future.
This post The Architecture of Mon...
content:
Money determines where we live, what we can afford, and how wealth accumulates across generations. Yet the mechanisms that create and distribute it remain largely occluded, even as their consequences become harder to unsee. For Dutch artist Carlijn Kingma, investigative financial journalist Thomas Bollen, and monetary researcher Martijn Jeroen van der Linden, that disconnect became the impetus for The Waterworks of Money. This ambitious project maps the hidden architecture of the financial system through drawing and animation, rendering it understandable to the people living within it without flattening its complexity.

The Waterworks of Money depicts the financial system as a vast network of reservoirs, channels, and pumps, revealing how money moves through banks, governments, businesses, and households. Some areas receive an abundance of liquidity, while others remain perpetually dry. The resulting drawing operates simultaneously as an artwork, an educational tool, and an examination of financial power.

The project emerged from two years of research, including interviews with more than 100 experts across banking, government, academia, and monetary reform movements. Kingma spent more than 2,200 hours translating that research into an intricate architectural landscape. Bollen, whose investigative journalism examines the workings of the financial system, and van der Linden, whose academic research explores money and monetary reform, helped develop the economic research and narratives behind the work.

One of the project’s scenarios explores a monetary future shaped by bitcoin. As bitcoin enters traditional finance, an alternative monetary system either challenges existing structures of financial power or eventually becomes part of them, and the project’s collaborators have watched both happen.

Ahead of Bitcoin Amsterdam, November 5-6, where Bollen joins two panels, I sat down with all three of the project’s collaborators to discuss making money visible, the relationship between monetary systems and inequality, and bitcoin’s place in Europe’s financial future.

BMAG: The Waterworks of Money illustrates the financial system as a network of reservoirs, pumps, and channels, with some parts of society receiving abundant liquidity while others remain dry. After two years of research and interviews with financial experts, what surprised you most about how money actually works? What do you think the public most fundamentally misunderstands about it?

Thomas Bollen: What surprised me most is that many people inside the system know a great deal about their own corner of it: interest rate derivatives, asset management or mortgage lending. Very few of them can oversee the larger system in which they operate.

What is clearly not well understood is that banks create new money when they make a loan. They are not just intermediaries that pass on the savings of their depositors.

But can you blame ordinary people for that? During the research phase we spoke to many bankers and even a CEO of a major bank who did not know they were working for a money creating institution.

If we want to improve understanding we should start at our schools and universities. Many textbooks still get it wrong, and economics education hardly pays any attention to it. In 2022 even the Riksbank’s prize in economics (the Nobel prize that is not really a Nobel prize) was awarded for research that presents banks as mere intermediaries.

BMAG: One of the central ideas in The Waterworks of Money is that money doesn’t flow evenly through society. Housing affordability has become a major issue in Europe and the United States, while asset prices and financial wealth have increasingly outpaced wages. How much of this inequality results from the design of our monetary system, rather than broader economic forces?

Thomas Bollen: It is impossible to capture that in a precise number, because so many factors play a role. But it is quite clear that the money system exacerbated inequality enormously during all those years when credit was extremely cheap.

Ray Dalio, founder of the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, summed it up in 2019: “Money is free for those who are creditworthy.” For everyone without money or creditworthiness, it was out of reach.

Cheap credit for rich people and large multinationals (who used it for share buybacks and M&A deals) drove up the price of shares, and of houses. Bank money creation produced a specific kind of inflation: asset inflation. Wealthy households and large multinationals, who already owned those assets, profited far more from it than people without them or small businesses that did not have the same kind of access to cheap credit as their larger competitors.

BMAG: The Waterworks of Money is filled with details that help explain how the financial system works. What was the most difficult part of the monetary system to illustrate? Did anything you learned during the research change how you approached the drawing?

Carlijn Kingma: The biggest challenge was the way all the parts are connected. How do you show that clearly?

Water is the obvious metaphor for money, and it takes you a long way. Liquidity, cash flows, money drying up: they are already in the language of finance. It was also great for connecting the different parts of the system, because I could draw the pipes and canals that run between them.

But in some places you need more than that if you want to be completely accurate. Money comes in many forms: commodity money, public money, private credit money, and further out short-term debt and repo contracts can also serve as money or near-money. It was not possible to draw that many different kinds of water running through the system.

BMAG: The Waterworks of Money has been shown to both art audiences and people interested in economics, including at Bitcoin Amsterdam last year. Have you noticed differences in how these audiences respond to the work? Has their feedback influenced how you think about the role of art in explaining complex ideas?

Carlijn Kingma: The response depends on what people already know. Visitors with more financial knowledge usually laugh more, because they catch all the small jokes. We renamed Basel III to “Babel III”, for instance, because the bank rules written after the crisis add up to about three bibles.

In our bitcoin future scenario, The Republic of a Thousand Coins, we put in a lot of jokes about central bankers. You can see Alan Greenspan there as an inflatable doll. That works best if you know who he is, and the bitcoin crowd knows far more about monetary history than the general public.

Above all, we noticed that art opens doors. The drawing gives people a visual starting point for a conversation. Even without any prior knowledge, the metaphor lets you see the social outcomes of how money flows.

BMAG: Your research has examined how financial crises can reinforce the influence of institutions considered too important to fail. More recently, you’ve explored the growing power of asset managers such as BlackRock and Vanguard. Are we witnessing a genuine transformation in how financial power operates, or have the same underlying problems simply taken new forms since 2008?

Martijn Jeroen van der Linden: Following the crisis of 2008, there was a general consensus among mainstream policymakers, think tanks and many economists that the banking sector needed to be repaired. In Europe, the influential de Larosière Group concluded that the causes of the crisis were excessive leverage, opaque securitisation, shadow banking risks, and fragmented supervision in the EU, and argued that “repair is necessary and urgent.” The banking repair consisted of new and stricter regulations, stronger coordinated supervision and new crisis management procedures. The underlying architecture remained unaltered, meaning that fundamental change never occurred.

But the architecture remained fragile. Take, for example, 2023. When Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse got into trouble, the crisis playbooks developed after 2008 stayed in the drawer. The US authorities guaranteed all SVB deposits, including the more than 90 percent above the insured limit. In Switzerland, the state backed the rescue of Credit Suisse by UBS.

Advocates of banking repair often claim to have made the system safer. But the inherent fragility of funding long-term loans with runnable bank deposits is still there. Even with all the regulation, you cannot prevent a bank run, and that fragility is precisely what they refuse to solve. The banking system only survives because of massive public safety nets and privileges given to banks.

Large powerful non-banks have indeed emerged but they do not play a pivotal role in money and payments. This is a key distinction between the two sectors.

BMAG: Bitcoin began as an attempt to create money outside the control of governments and banks. Today, it’s increasingly held through investment funds and traditional financial institutions, including some of the same powerful asset managers examined in your recent work. Does this integration strengthen bitcoin’s ability to change the financial system, or risk reproducing the concentration of power it originally sought to challenge?

Martijn Jeroen van der Linden: As a financial asset, bitcoin has benefited from investments from traditional financial institutions. But the increasing use of bitcoin as an investment has compromised its promise of an alternative payment system.

At the same time, bitcoin and the rise of stablecoins have challenged the banks on their payment infrastructure. The banks are now innovating too: look at Wero, the payment wallet that a group of European banks launched in 2024. That is a change. But it is something different from the structural reform of money and banking.

BMAG: Your project imagines bitcoin as an alternative to the existing monetary system. Amsterdam also has a remarkable history of monetary experimentation, from the development of modern financial institutions to David Chaum’s pioneering work on private digital cash decades before bitcoin. Given that history, how do you see bitcoin’s role in Europe’s financial future? Has your perspective changed since you began working on the project?

Thomas Bollen: What I appreciate about bitcoin’s design is that it resembles full reserve banking. A bitcoin is not a claim on something else, so it carries no risk of a bank run. Bank deposits are: they are a promise that you can withdraw your money at any moment, while the bank can never keep that promise to all its customers at once.

We can learn a lot from our history. The Amsterdamsche Wisselbank, founded in 1609 and often seen as the world’s first central bank, started out as a full reserve bank: every bank guilder was backed by coins in its vault. It went under only after it secretly began lending more and more to the Dutch East India Company.

That is the risk of every monetary experiment: it can go in the wrong direction. In the crypto world, all kinds of companies started copying the banks. They lent out their customers’ bitcoins, while those customers still saw their coin-balances in their accounts. Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX shows how this practice can go horribly wrong.
